segments.text: In this video, we will be visiting this question and looking at how to draw the free-body diagram for it.
Everything else in this question, we will visit in a later video when we have learned about gravity, normal force, and friction.
But first of all, let's see. The question first wants to draw a free-body diagram.
And a free-body diagram is basically a diagram that shows and demonstrates all the forces acting on an object, in this case, the crate.
So let's see the question. A five kilogram crate is placed on a rough horizontal floor.
The crate is pulled to the right by a net force of 18 newtons. Sorry, not net, by a horizontal force of 18 newtons.
The coefficient of kinetic friction between the crate and the floor is, we don't need to know that, we will learn that later.
But first of all, let's draw all the forces acting on the crate.
The first thing you want to think of when drawing all the forces is, in most questions, in 99% of the questions, unless it occurs in space, there will always be a gravity component.
And we would call that FG, or we can sometimes denote that as MG, depends on how you want to portray that.
Next, what we have is something called the normal force. Why is there a normal force?
Well, remember Newton's third law. For every action, there's an equal and opposite reaction.
So if the box is leaning on the floor and it exerts a force of FG on the floor because of its weight,
then there will be an equal and opposite reaction that the floor exerts back on that box.
And we will call that F normal. Without this normal force, the box will just slide down through the box.
Next, we have it being pulled to the right by a horizontal force of 18 Newton's.
I forgot to mention that most of the times forces are denoted from the center when we're talking about things like external forces, for example, in this case, or gravity.
So over here we have a force. Let's call this force applied.
You can denote this whatever you want, but usually it would be applied force. And this is 18 Newton's.
And now we need another force because it's a rough horizontal floor. So there will be a friction force.
I'll denote this friction force coming from here because it's between the floor and the box.
You can also do it here. Really doesn't matter, but putting it here would make it more accurate and make it easier to visualize.
And we could call this F of friction. And that is basically free body diagrams.
How about let's have another example down here. Let's say we have a ball.
Let's say this would be the diagram that's not free body, just a normal diagram.
Now, let's say this is a pendulum and the ball starts from here and it's going to go swing back and forth.
Now, what are the forces acting on this ball? Let's draw it out in a free body diagram here.
First of all, as always, there's gravity. And to counteract that gravity, there's also going to be a tension force that partially counteracts that.
So we would call that F t and F g. There will also be air resistance, but in most problems at this level, we won't need to take into account.
The problem will probably say air resistance is neglected, so we can ignore that.
Sometimes it's going to give you the angle at which the pendulum is released. We'll get into that in another unit.
But that angle is the same as the angle on a free body diagram, which makes a free body diagram really, really useful for calculating these things.
And that's it for an introduction of free body diagrams. Remember, there will always be gravity.
There will usually be a normal force, especially if it's on a surface and you do applied forces starting from the middle.
Thank you guys for watching.
